# Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding

Zijun Huang Affiliation: University of Southern California    Yingjun Du
^(†)^(†)thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: VisLab, University of
Amsterdam    Cees Snoek Affiliation: VisLab, University of Amsterdam

###### Abstract

Vision-language verifiers judge whether an image faithfully matches a
textual description, yet existing training pipelines typically rely on
static supervision from stronger external judges or curated
hard-negative data. Such supervision requires external generation or
annotation, is teacher-bounded, and is difficult to adapt as model
failures evolve. We introduce PROVE (Perturb-and-Repair Optimization for
Vision-Language Evaluation), a self-play framework that trains verifiers
through a closed perturb–verify–repair–verify loop. Starting from a
known-correct image-caption pair, a Mutator introduces a typed
perturbation over objects, attributes, counts, or relations. The
verifier then judges the perturbed caption and provides textual
feedback, which a Repairer uses to recover a faithful caption for
re-verification. These two verification rounds produce structured
rewards for informative mismatches and visually grounded repairs. Since
perturbation, verification, and repair are role-conditioned behaviors of
the same evolving multimodal backbone, updating the shared parameters
also improves the verifier itself. Experiments show that PROVE improves
fine-grained compositional verification across model scales and families
and strengthens visual-detail robustness on the reference backbone, with
limited, benchmark-dependent changes on broader multimodal tasks.

## 1 Introduction

Vision-language models have made rapid progress in image-text
understanding, yet they still often miss subtle but consequential
mismatches between an image and a textual description. A caption may
differ from the image by a substituted object, a misbound attribute, an
incorrect count, or a reversed relation, while still retaining high
global semantic similarity. As illustrated in
Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")[1(a)](#S1.F1.sf1 "In Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding"),
these errors lie along fine-grained visual-semantic axes that are
difficult to capture with coarse image-text scores. This limitation is
especially important because VLMs are increasingly used as _verifiers_:
given an image and a description, the verifier judges whether the
description faithfully matches the image. Such verifiers support
VLM-as-judge evaluation \[[49](#bib.bib28)\], reward modeling for
RLHF \[[29](#bib.bib30)\] and RLAIF \[[16](#bib.bib29)\],
generated-image filtering, and hallucination
detection \[[19](#bib.bib20), [9](#bib.bib22)\]. A central question is
therefore how to train verifiers that recognize localized image-text
misalignment, rather than merely score global semantic compatibility.

The dominant recipe imports supervision from outside the target model,
as summarized in
Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")[1(b)](#S1.F1.sf2 "In Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding").
A stronger reference judge, typically a larger VLM or a curated process
reward model, scores candidate image-text pairs, and the target verifier
is trained to imitate or optimize against that score \[[46](#bib.bib9),
[39](#bib.bib12), [20](#bib.bib14)\]. Alternatively, training relies on
human-labeled or synthetically generated hard
negatives \[[17](#bib.bib49), [30](#bib.bib37), [14](#bib.bib50)\].
Although effective, both routes provide _static_ supervision. The
student is bounded by the perceptual distinctions exposed by the
external judge or negative set; the supervision may lag behind evolving
model failures; and extending verification to new axes such as counting,
relations, or attribute binding often requires new annotation or
generation pipelines. The core challenge is to obtain image-text
mismatches that are simultaneously _grounded_ in the image, _hard_
enough to train fine-grained discrimination, and _gradable_ without
relying on a stronger external judge.

We introduce PROVE (Perturb-and-Repair Optimization for Vision-Language
Evaluation), a self-play framework that trains a verifier through a
closed perturb–verify–repair–verify loop
(Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")[1(c)](#S1.F1.sf3 "In Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")).
Starting from a known-correct image-caption pair, a Mutator creates a
minimally perturbed caption by editing one visual-semantic axis, such as
object identity, attribute, count, or relation. The verifier then judges
the perturbed caption and provides feedback about the mismatch.
Conditioned on this feedback, a Repairer attempts to recover a faithful
caption, which is verified again. Crucially, perturbation, verification,
and repair are not separate models: they are three role-conditioned
behaviors of the same evolving VLM. The two verification rounds produce
rewards for informative perturbations and visually grounded repairs,
while shared-parameter updates also improve the verifier used at
evaluation time.

Figure 1: Motivation of PROVE. (a) Fine-grained image-text verification

This formulation is well matched to fine-grained image-text
verification. The Mutator does not generate arbitrary text corruptions;
it creates controlled, localized mismatches whose semantic axes mirror
common compositional failures. The verifier must diagnose the mismatch
before repair and recognize the corrected caption after repair, while
the Repairer must localize the error and infer the visually faithful
description. In this way, PROVE converts ordinary clean image-caption
pairs into adaptive hard negatives and repair targets. Compared with
external-judge distillation, the training signal is not bounded by a
stronger frozen oracle. Compared with fixed hard-negative training, the
mismatch distribution evolves with the current verifier.

We evaluate PROVE on a Qwen3.5-2B backbone across fine-grained
compositional alignment benchmarks and broader vision-language
robustness benchmarks. PROVE consistently improves the same backbone on
compositional verification, with the largest gains appearing on axes
aligned with the perturbation space, such as attribute and relation
understanding. It also improves visual-detail sensitivity and maintains
hallucination robustness, while broader capability changes are limited
and benchmark-dependent. Training diagnostics further show that
perturbation and repair co-adapt through verifier feedback. These
results suggest that vision-language verifiers can be strengthened
through verifier-guided self-play rather than static judge distillation.

Matched supervision baselines, independent verifier audits, and
additional Qwen3.5-4B and InternVL3-2B experiments further support this
teacher-free adaptive alternative. The present study establishes
caption-based verification and benchmark transfer; task-specific
self-play for VQA, grounding, and referring expressions remains future
work.

## 2 Related Work

Vision-language verifiers for image-text understanding. Evaluating
whether an image faithfully matches a textual description is a central
problem in vision-language understanding. Coarse image-text similarity
metrics are often insufficient, because they can miss fine-grained
errors in object identity, attribute binding, counting, and spatial
relations. Recent work therefore uses vision-language models as
verifiers or judges for multimodal evaluation, reward modeling,
generated-image filtering, and hallucination
detection \[[49](#bib.bib28), [19](#bib.bib20), [9](#bib.bib22),
[8](#bib.bib3)\]. These verifiers are attractive because they can
provide semantic judgments beyond fixed embedding similarities, but
their reliability depends on whether they can detect subtle image-text
mismatches. PROVE targets this capability directly by training the
verifier through controlled perturbation, verification, and repair over
the same compositional axes that commonly challenge image-text
understanding.

Training verifiers with static external supervision. A common way to
train multimodal verifiers is to import supervision from outside the
target model. For example, stronger VLMs or curated reward models can
score candidate image-text pairs, after which the target model is
optimized by preference learning or reward-based
training \[[46](#bib.bib9), [39](#bib.bib12), [18](#bib.bib13),
[20](#bib.bib14), [38](#bib.bib2), [37](#bib.bib1)\]. Another line
constructs fixed hard-negative datasets or synthetic preference pairs,
then trains the verifier to distinguish faithful captions from
controlled corruptions \[[21](#bib.bib11)\]. These approaches provide
useful supervision, but the signal is static: it is bounded by the
external judge, fixed negative generator, or annotation pipeline. As
models and evaluation distributions evolve, their failure modes may
shift away from this supervision. In contrast, PROVE does not distill a
stronger frozen judge or rely on a fixed hard-negative set. It uses the
current verifier itself inside a perturb–verify–repair–verify loop, so
the training signal changes with the evolving model.

Self-play and self-evolving multimodal learning. Self-play has been
widely used to improve agents and reasoning systems, from game-playing
methods such as AlphaZero \[[36](#bib.bib7)\] to debate and recent
self-evolving LLMs \[[13](#bib.bib8), [12](#bib.bib5),
[47](#bib.bib6)\]. More recent asymmetric self-play methods train one
behavior to propose tasks and another to solve them, creating an
adaptive curriculum without a fixed external
teacher \[[23](#bib.bib4)\]. In multimodal learning, self-evolving VLMs
have also been explored through questioner–reasoner interactions and
pseudo-labeling from model samples \[[10](#bib.bib10)\]. However,
consensus- or uncertainty-based supervision can still reinforce
confident mistakes, especially when the model fails to perceive the
relevant visual evidence. PROVE differs in both task and interaction
structure: it trains a vision-language verifier rather than a general
reasoner, and it grounds self-play in clean image-caption pairs. The
Mutator creates typed image-text mismatches, the verifier diagnoses
them, and the Repairer attempts to correct them; all three are
role-conditioned behaviors of the same evolving MLLM.

Compositional image-text alignment. Vision-language models often
struggle with compositional understanding despite strong global
image-text alignment. Benchmarks such as
Winoground \[[40](#bib.bib15)\], ARO \[[44](#bib.bib16)\],
SugarCrepe \[[11](#bib.bib17)\], and VL-CheckList \[[48](#bib.bib19)\]
test whether models can distinguish captions that differ in objects,
attributes, relations, or word order. Prior methods improve this ability
with hard-negative contrastive learning or synthetic
data \[[44](#bib.bib16), [7](#bib.bib18)\]. PROVE is complementary: it
generates controlled perturbations online and uses verifier-guided
repair to create adaptive supervision for fine-grained image-text
alignment.

## 3 Methods

### 3.1 Overview

PROVE trains a vision-language verifier through a closed
perturb–verify–repair–verify loop. Given a clean image-caption pair, a
single multimodal policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ is reused under three role
prompts: a Mutator that perturbs the caption, a Verifier that judges
image-caption faithfulness, and a Repairer that corrects the caption
using verifier feedback. These roles are not separate models; they are
three behaviors of the same parameter-shared backbone. Thus, every
policy update also changes the verifier used at evaluation time.
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Overview ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
illustrates the overall loop.

The key idea is to turn ordinary positive image-caption pairs into
adaptive verification episodes. The Mutator creates localized mismatches
along object, attribute, count, or relation axes. The Verifier diagnoses
whether the perturbed caption still matches the image. The Repairer then
attempts to recover a faithful caption from the image and verifier
feedback. This interaction produces grounded hard negatives and repair
targets without a stronger external judge or a fixed hard-negative
dataset.

![Refer to caption](2611.05158v1/fig2_overview.png)

Figure 2: Overview of PROVE. A single Qwen backbone is reused under
three role prompts: Mutator, Verifier, and Repairer. Given a clean
image-caption pair, the Mutator produces a localized caption
perturbation, e.g., changing an attribute from “red” to “blue”, to
create a hard image-text mismatch. The Verifier first judges the
perturbed caption and returns a decision-feedback pair $`(y_{1},r_{1})`$
that diagnoses the mismatch. Conditioned on this feedback, the Repairer
generates a revised caption, which is then checked by the same Verifier
to obtain $`(y_{2},r_{2})`$. Rewards from the two verification rounds
train the shared model with DrGRPO, so perturbation, verification, and
repair co-evolve within one multimodal backbone.

### 3.2 Perturb–Verify–Repair–Verify Self-Play

Let $`\mathcal{D}=\{(x_{i},p_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}`$ be a set of
image-caption pairs, where $`p_{i}`$ faithfully describes image
$`x_{i}`$. For a clean pair $`(x,p)`$, PROVE constructs the following
self-play episode:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
(x,p)\;\xrightarrow{\text{Mutator }}\;p^{\prime}\;\xrightarrow{\text{Verifier}}\;(y_{1},r_{1})\;\xrightarrow{\text{Repairer }}\;\tilde{p}\;\xrightarrow{\text{Verifier}}\;(y_{2},r_{2}).
``` |  | (1) |

Here $`p^{\prime}`$ is a perturbed caption, $`(y_{1},r_{1})`$ is the
first verifier decision and explanation, $`\tilde{p}`$ is the repaired
caption, and $`(y_{2},r_{2})`$ is the second verifier decision and
explanation. The binary label $`y\in\{0,1\}`$ indicates whether the
caption is judged faithful to the image, and $`r`$ is natural-language
feedback.

All stages are sampled from the same policy under different role
prompts:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,q,z),\qquad z\in\{\textsc{Mutator},\textsc{Verifier},\textsc{Repairer}\},
``` |  | (2) |

where $`q`$ denotes the role-specific text context. This makes the
verifier part of the evolving policy, rather than a frozen reward model.

##### Caption perturbation.

The Mutator produces a localized edit

|     |                        |     |     |
|-----|------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       a_{M}=(\tau,t,\delta),
       ```                     |     | (3) |

where $`\tau`$ is the edit type, $`t`$ is the target span, and
$`\delta`$ specifies the replacement. We use four edit types:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{T}=\{\textsf{object},\textsf{attribute},\textsf{count},\textsf{relation}\}.
``` |  | (4) |

A deterministic editor applies the edit to obtain the perturbed caption:

|     |                        |     |     |
|-----|------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       p^{\prime}=E(p,a_{M}).
       ```                     |     | (5) |

Restricting the Mutator to typed local edits prevents arbitrary
rewriting and keeps the negative caption close to the original
image-caption pair. Invalid edit types, unmatched or ambiguous target
spans, unchanged replacements, and non-deterministic edits are filtered;
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Role Interfaces and Deterministic Editing ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
describes the role interfaces and editor constraints.

##### Verification and repair.

The Verifier first judges the perturbed caption:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(y_{1},r_{1})\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,p^{\prime},\textsc{Verifier}).
``` |  | (6) |

The feedback $`r_{1}`$ identifies the perceived mismatch and is passed
to the Repairer, which generates a corrected caption:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\tilde{p}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,p^{\prime},y_{1},r_{1},\textsc{Repairer}).
``` |  | (7) |

The same Verifier then evaluates the repaired caption:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(y_{2},r_{2})\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,\tilde{p},\textsc{Verifier}).
``` |  | (8) |

The first verification tests whether the model detects the perturbation;
the second tests whether the repair restores faithfulness. Together,
they turn verification into an operational correction task.

### 3.3 Verifier-Guided Rewards

The two verifier calls provide the supervision for self-play. The
Mutator should produce perturbations that are informative, grounded, and
not overly destructive. The Repairer should recover a faithful caption
while making minimal changes.

##### Mutator reward.

We define the Mutator reward as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{M}=R_{\mathrm{expose}}(y_{1})+R_{\mathrm{hard}}(y_{2})-\lambda_{M}C_{M}(a_{M}),
``` |  | (9) |

where $`R_{\mathrm{expose}}`$ rewards perturbations that expose verifier
blind spots, $`R_{\mathrm{hard}}`$ rewards perturbations that remain
difficult after repair, and $`C_{M}`$ penalizes overly wide edits.
Invalid actions receive a fixed penalty and do not enter $`C_{M}`$
(Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Role Interfaces and Deterministic Editing ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")).
We instantiate it as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{M}=\lambda_{1}\mathbb{1}[y_{1}=1]+\lambda_{2}\mathbb{1}[y_{2}=0]-\lambda_{3}C_{M}(a_{M}).
``` |  | (10) |

##### Repairer reward.

The Repairer reward encourages a successful and minimal correction:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{R}=R_{\mathrm{accept}}(y_{2})+R_{\mathrm{flip}}(y_{1},y_{2})-\lambda_{R}C_{R}(p^{\prime},\tilde{p}),
``` |  | (11) |

where $`R_{\mathrm{accept}}`$ rewards repaired captions accepted by the
verifier, $`R_{\mathrm{flip}}`$ rewards changing the verifier judgment,
and $`C_{R}`$ penalizes unnecessary rewriting. We use

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{R}=\beta_{1}\mathbb{1}[y_{2}=1]+\beta_{2}\mathbb{1}[y_{1}\neq y_{2}]-\beta_{3}C_{R}(p^{\prime},\tilde{p}).
``` |  | (12) |

Although rewards are assigned to perturbation and repair trajectories,
the Verifier is not a frozen judge. Because all roles share $`\theta`$,
updates from these rewards also update the verifier behavior itself.
This coupling is what allows PROVE to improve the verifier without
distilling a stronger external model.

### 3.4 Role-Conditioned Policy Optimization

We optimize the shared policy with DrGRPO \[[27](#bib.bib32)\]. For each
source pair, the model samples multiple self-play trajectories and
computes verifier-guided rewards. Let $`r_{i}`$ be the reward of
trajectory $`i`$, and let $`G(i)`$ be the group of trajectories sampled
from the same source context. Following DrGRPO, we use mean-centered
advantages without standard-deviation normalization:

|     |                                                          |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \hat{A}_{i}=r_{i}-\frac{1}{|G(i)|}\sum_{j\in G(i)}r_{j}.
       ```                                                       |     | (13) |

This preserves the reward scale and avoids unstable rescaling when
within-group variance is small.

The clipped objective over generated tokens is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{i,t}\left[\min\left(\rho_{i,t}(\theta)\hat{A}_{i},\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\rho_{i,t}(\theta),1-\epsilon^{-},1+\epsilon^{+}\right)\hat{A}_{i}\right)\right],
``` |  | (14) |

where

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\rho_{i,t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_{i,t}\mid q_{i},a_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a_{i,t}\mid q_{i},a_{i,<t})}.
``` |  | (15) |

Here $`q_{i}`$ is the role-conditioned multimodal prompt and $`a_{i,t}`$
is the generated token.
Equation [14](#S3.E14 "In 3.4 Role-Conditioned Policy Optimization ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
is a maximization objective; equivalently, its negative is minimized,
with KL regularization specified in the experimental setup. At test
time, we use the Verifier prompt of the evolved shared model to judge
image-caption faithfulness.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

Backbone and training framework. We instantiate PROVE with
Qwen3.5-2B \[[31](#bib.bib33)\] as the shared multimodal backbone. The
same parameters are reused across the Mutator, Verifier, and Repairer
roles, with role identity specified only by the prompt template. Thus,
perturbation, verification, and repair are optimized as role-conditioned
behaviors of one evolving MLLM rather than as separate models. At
evaluation time, we use the Verifier role of the evolved shared model to
judge image-caption faithfulness.

Training data and self-play construction. We train on a 48k-example
subset of ShareGPT-4o-Image-style image-caption
pairs \[[4](#bib.bib34)\], with a held-out validation split of 5k
examples. Each self-play episode starts from a known-correct
image-caption pair. The Mutator introduces a typed perturbation along
one of four visual-semantic axes: object, attribute, count, or relation.
The Verifier then judges the perturbed caption and produces a
decision-feedback pair. Conditioned on this feedback, the Repairer
generates a repaired caption, which is judged again by the same Verifier
role. The two verification rounds provide verifier-guided rewards for
self-play optimization. No stronger external judge, human-labeled hard
negatives, or additional hard-negative annotations are used during
training.

Optimization and compute. We implement PROVE using the VeRL/HybridFlow
training framework \[[35](#bib.bib35)\] and optimize the shared policy
with DrGRPO \[[27](#bib.bib32)\], a group-relative policy optimization
variant that removes the standard-deviation normalization used in
vanilla GRPO \[[34](#bib.bib31)\]. Unless otherwise specified, we use
rollout size $`n=3`$, learning rate $`5\times 10^{-7}`$, global batch
size 48, KL coefficient $`0.005`$, and PPO clip range $`[0.20,0.22]`$.
All main training runs are conducted on a single node with 8 NVIDIA A100
GPUs using BF16 mixed precision. We report the best validation
checkpoint in the main results. Training hyperparameters, role
interfaces, and additional experimental results are provided in the
appendix. The reference run takes 11 hours on 8 A100 GPUs (88
GPU-hours);
Appendix [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Compute Cost ‣ Appendix A Additional Experimental Details ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
compares complete pipeline costs. We will release the training and
evaluation code to facilitate reproducibility.

Evaluation protocol. Our main evaluation focuses on fine-grained
image-text understanding, where a verifier must distinguish captions
that differ by localized semantic changes.
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
compares PROVE with representative compositional understanding methods
on four benchmarks shared with \[[30](#bib.bib37)\]:
ARO \[[44](#bib.bib16)\], VL-CheckList \[[48](#bib.bib19)\],
ColorSwap \[[3](#bib.bib47)\], and FG-OVD \[[1](#bib.bib48)\]. These
benchmarks cover relation and attribute reasoning, object-level
grounding, color-word order sensitivity, and fine-grained
open-vocabulary recognition. For each baseline, we report the values
published in the original paper whenever available; when a benchmark was
not reported but public code is available, we use our reproduction under
the same evaluation protocol.

Beyond the core compositional suites, we evaluate how the learned
verifier transfers to broader vision-language understanding. We include
Winoground \[[40](#bib.bib15)\] to test role binding under hard
image-text contrasts, MMVP \[[41](#bib.bib21)\] to assess sensitivity to
fine visual details, and MMBench-EN \[[25](#bib.bib23)\] to measure
general multimodal perception and reasoning. For all two-alternative
forced-choice tasks, we randomize option order for each example to
reduce positional bias. Unless otherwise stated, all benchmarks are
evaluated using their official protocols and metrics. Comp. Avg.
averages the four core benchmark groups in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding");
Broader Avg. averages Winoground GS, MMVP pair accuracy, and MMBench in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding").
Winoground GS and the appendix 2-AFC accuracy are distinct metrics.
External evaluation labels are not used for training, rewards, mutation
generation, validation, or checkpoint selection.

achieves the best average and improves the Qwen3.5-2B backbone on all
three benchmarks, indicating transfer beyond the core compositional
suites. Broader task changes are benchmark-dependent
(Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Repeated-Run Variability and Broader Capability ‣ Appendix C Independent Verification and Repeated-Run Analysis ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")).

Compositional understanding.
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
compares PROVE with representative compositional understanding methods
on ARO, VL-CheckList, ColorSwap, and FG-OVD. Because these methods
differ in backbone architecture, training data, objectives, and
benchmark coverage, the cross-method comparison should be interpreted as
a contextual reference rather than a fully controlled comparison. Our
main controlled comparison is between Qwen3.5-2B and PROVE using the
same backbone. Under this controlled setting, PROVE improves the overall
average from 83.22 to 86.85, with consistent gains across all four
benchmark groups. The largest improvement appears on ARO, where the
average score increases by $`+7.25`$, indicating stronger attribute and
relation discrimination. PROVE also improves VL-CheckList, ColorSwap,
and FG-OVD, suggesting that the learned verifier benefits not only the
perturbation axes seen during self-play but also broader forms of
localized image-text grounding. Compared with prior compositional
methods, PROVE achieves the best overall average among complete rows in
this table and remains competitive on individual benchmark groups,
despite using a compact shared backbone and no external hard-negative
dataset. These results support the core design of PROVE. The Mutator
creates controlled mismatches over objects, attributes, counts, and
relations; the Verifier learns to diagnose these mismatches; and the
Repairer learns to recover visually faithful captions. The resulting
self-play signal strengthens fine-grained image-text verification
without relying on a stronger external judge.

Broader vision-language understanding benchmarks.
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
evaluates whether the learned verifier transfers beyond the main
compositional suites. PROVE improves the Qwen3.5-2B backbone on all
three benchmarks, raising the average from 58.77 to 61.03. The most
notable gain is on MMVP, where pair accuracy improves by $`+4.00`$,
suggesting improved sensitivity to fine visual details. Winoground also
improves, indicating better role binding under hard image-text
contrasts, while MMBench-EN shows a modest positive change, suggesting
positive transfer to this general multimodal perception and reasoning
benchmark.

Together,
Tables [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
and [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
show that PROVE mainly strengthens the verifier on localized image-text
discrimination, which matches the intended training signal of typed
perturbation and verifier-guided repair. At the same time, the gains on
MMVP and MMBench indicate positive transfer, while repeated-run results
reveal small, task-dependent regressions on other broader benchmarks
(Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Repeated-Run Variability and Broader Capability ‣ Appendix C Independent Verification and Repeated-Run Analysis ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")).

Matched supervision alternatives.
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
compares static negatives generated once, judgments from a frozen larger

the compositional/broader averages over these baselines by
$`1.83/1.35`$, $`0.56/0.31`$, and $`1.19/0.82`$ points, respectively.
These results support adaptive perturb–repair self-play as a
teacher-free alternative; its advantage is adaptive supervision rather
than uniformly lower compute or universal superiority over distillation.

### 4.3 Analysis

Self-Play Dynamics Analysis.
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")(a)
analyzes how the perturb–verify–repair loop evolves during training. The
training dynamics show that the Repairer steadily catches up with the
perturbations produced by the Mutator while the overall optimization
remains stable. Repair success increases from $`36.0\%`$ to $`62.7\%`$,
and structural alignment rises from $`61.0\%`$ to $`78.6\%`$, indicating
that the Repairer becomes increasingly capable of localizing
Mutator-induced mismatches and recovering visually faithful captions. At
the same time, the verifier pass rate increases from $`0.360`$ to
$`0.633`$ and remains above the lower finite-group maximum-variance
reference point of $`1/3`$, suggesting that the current four-type
perturbation space gradually becomes easier for the evolving Repairer to
solve. This trend reveals both the effectiveness and the limitation of
the current self-play curriculum: typed perturbations provide a useful
learning signal, but a richer action vocabulary may be needed once the
Repairer becomes strong enough to saturate the existing perturbation
space. Finally, the validation reward improves consistently, suggesting
that the verifier-guided rewards provide a stable learning signal.

Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")(b)
summarizes where the gains of PROVE come from by aggregating benchmark

largest improvements appear on attribute and relation verification,
which are directly aligned with the typed perturbations used by the
Mutator. The full analysis is provided in
Appendix [G.1](#A7.SS1 "G.1 Axis-level Gains ‣ Appendix G Axis-level Gains, Qualitative Behavior, and Task Extensions ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding").

Controlled loop ablations. Removing the Repairer and second verification
lowers the two averages by $`2.61/1.72`$ points; removing verifier
feedback costs $`1.68/1.19`$
(Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")).
Freezing the internal Verifier costs $`1.73/1.22`$, supporting verifier
co-evolution. Reward and role-sharing ablations also favor the full
loop, while replacing DrGRPO with GRPO costs only $`0.43/0.32`$
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Controlled Supervision and Loop Ablations ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")).

Independent verification.
Table [12](#A3.T12 "Table 12 ‣ C.1 External Trajectory Audit ‣ Appendix C Independent Verification and Repeated-Run Analysis ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
shows a $`7.8`$-point verifier accuracy gain and a $`23.4`$-point
increase in fully valid trajectories, requiring a real mismatch, correct
diagnosis, faithful minimal repair, and correct final judgment. Fixed
external benchmark averages also improve by $`3.63/2.26`$ points across
training; their correlations with self-play pass rate are
$`0.9254/0.9022`$
(Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 External Benchmark Trajectory ‣ Appendix C Independent Verification and Repeated-Run Analysis ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")).
These independent measurements support improved image-grounded
correctness beyond internal role agreement.

Generality and capability boundary.
Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
shows gains of $`3.56/2.34`$ on Qwen3.5-4B and $`3.15/2.83`$ on
InternVL3-2B. Three Qwen3.5-2B runs yield a compositional average of
$`86.73\pm 0.27`$, but ViVerBench, MMMU, and MathVista regress while
MMBench improves and POPE remains stable
(Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Repeated-Run Variability and Broader Capability ‣ Appendix C Independent Verification and Repeated-Run Analysis ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")).
Multi-edit curricula, unseen perturbation types, and caption filtering
are studied in
Appendices [D](#A4 "Appendix D Generality and Perturbation Curricula ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
and [E](#A5 "Appendix E Positive-Caption Quality ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding").
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
illustrates the learned verifier behavior. Additional failure analysis
and task extensions are provided in
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G Axis-level Gains, Qualitative Behavior, and Task Extensions ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding").

Limitations. PROVE uses four types of localized caption perturbations,
which align with the evaluated compositional axes and may saturate as
the Repairer improves. Although independent audits support improved
visual correctness, an evolving shared Verifier can still reinforce its
own perceptual mistakes. Training depends on faithful starting captions
from one corpus and requires four role-conditioned calls per trajectory,
increasing compute relative to static supervision. Broader capability
changes are benchmark-dependent, including regressions on ViVerBench,
MMMU, and MathVista. Task-specific self-play for VQA, grounding, and
referring expressions remains untested. Imperfect verifiers can also
propagate errors when used for automated evaluation or filtering; these
uses require independent validation.

## 5 Conclusion

We introduced PROVE, a self-play framework for training vision-language
verifiers through a closed perturb–verify–repair–verify loop. Instead of
relying on stronger external judges, fixed hard-negative datasets, or
static preference annotations, PROVE converts ordinary clean
image-caption pairs into adaptive verification episodes. A single shared
MLLM acts as a Mutator, Verifier, and Repairer under different role
prompts: the Mutator creates localized image-text mismatches, the
Verifier diagnoses them, and the Repairer attempts to recover faithful
captions from visual evidence and verifier feedback. This design turns
verification into an operational self-improvement problem, where the
model learns not only to judge image-text faithfulness but also to
expose and correct its own fine-grained failure modes. The resulting
training signal is grounded, adaptive, and verifier-guided. Typed
perturbations over objects, attributes, counts, and relations provide
controllable supervision for compositional understanding, while the two
verification rounds produce rewards that update the same backbone used
at test time. Experiments on Qwen3.5-2B, Qwen3.5-4B, and InternVL3-2B
backbones show that PROVE improves fine-grained compositional
understanding across multiple benchmarks. On the reference backbone, it
also strengthens visual-detail sensitivity, with limited,
benchmark-dependent changes on broader multimodal tasks. These results
suggest that self-play over perturbation, verification, and repair
offers a practical alternative to static judge distillation for building
stronger vision-language verifiers.

run. The same shared backbone is used for the Mutator, Verifier, and
Repairer roles, with role identity specified by prompt templates.

|--------------------------------------|----------------------------|
| Hyperparameter                       | Value                      |
| Backbone                             | Qwen3.5-2B                 |
| Training data                        | 48k image-caption pairs    |
| Validation data                      | 5k image-caption pairs     |

| rollout batch size                   | 48                         |
| rollout size $`n`$                   | 3                          |
| sampling temperature / top-p / top-k | 0.7 / 0.8 / 20             |
| presence penalty                     | 1.5                        |
| actor learning rate                  | $`5\times 10^{-7}`$        |
| global batch size                    | 48                         |
| PPO clip range                       | $`[0.20,0.22]`$            |
| KL coefficient $`\beta`$             | $`0.005`$                  |
| invalid-action penalty               | $`-0.3`$                   |
| precision                            | BF16                       |
| hardware                             | 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs         |
| reported checkpoint                  | best validation checkpoint |

Table 5: Training hyperparameters for the Qwen3.5-2B reference run.

### A.3 Reward Design Discussion

The verifier-guided rewards in PROVE are designed to couple two
complementary goals: exposing verifier weaknesses and recovering
faithful captions. For the Mutator, the reward contains an exposure
term, a hardness term, and an edit-cost penalty. The exposure term
encourages perturbations that the current verifier fails to reject,
while the hardness term encourages perturbations that remain challenging
after repair. The cost term discourages overly wide edits. Actions
rejected by the deterministic editor receive a fixed penalty instead of
$`C_{M}`$
(Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Role Interfaces and Deterministic Editing ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")).

For the Repairer, the reward contains an acceptance term, a
judgment-flip term, and a repair-cost penalty. The acceptance term
encourages repaired captions that the verifier judges faithful, while
the judgment-flip term rewards a change in the verifier decision,
$`\mathbb{1}[y_{1}\neq y_{2}]`$; the separate acceptance term favors a
faithful accepted repair. The repair-cost penalty discourages
unnecessary rewriting and encourages localized correction.

Table [8](#A1.T8 "Table 8 ‣ A.3 Reward Design Discussion ‣ Appendix A Additional Experimental Details ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
summarizes the role of each reward component.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
| Role | Component | Purpose |
| Mutator | $`R_{\mathrm{expose}}(y_{1})`$ | Expose verifier blind spots |
| Mutator | $`R_{\mathrm{hard}}(y_{2})`$ | Prefer perturbations that remain challenging after repair |
| Mutator | $`C_{M}(a_{M})`$ | Penalize overly wide edits |
| Mutator | invalid-action penalty | Fixed penalty when the editor rejects the action |
| Repairer | $`R_{\mathrm{accept}}(y_{2})`$ | Reward repaired captions accepted by the verifier |
| Repairer | $`R_{\mathrm{flip}}(y_{1},y_{2})`$ | Reward a change in the verifier judgment |
| Repairer | $`C_{R}(p^{\prime},\tilde{p})`$ | Penalize unnecessary rewriting |

Table 8: Verifier-guided reward components in PROVE.

### A.4 Compute Cost

The Qwen3.5-2B reference run is trained on a single node with 8 NVIDIA
A100 GPUs using BF16 mixed precision. Each self-play episode executes
the perturb–verify–repair–verify trajectory with one shared backbone
under different role prompts. The main run uses rollout size $`n=3`$ and
global batch size 48; the reported trajectory includes checkpoints
through step 750. The reference run takes 11 hours on 8 A100 GPUs,
totaling 88 GPU-hours. We will release the training and evaluation code,
including launch scripts and prompt templates, to facilitate
reproducibility.

We profile all complete pipelines on the same hardware and 48k source
pairs
(Table [9](#A1.T9 "Table 9 ‣ A.4 Compute Cost ‣ Appendix A Additional Experimental Details ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")).
For PROVE, supervision is generated online and is included in
target-training time. Its four role-conditioned calls per trajectory
produce more generated tokens than either static negatives or offline
external-judge distillation. Thus, the benefit is adaptive supervision
without a separate teacher or fixed negative set, rather than
universally lower raw compute.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Method |     Supervision  generation |     Target  training |     Total  GPU-hours |     Generated  tokens/source |
| Fixed typed negatives | 4.8 | 43.2 | 48.0 | 46 |
| External-judge distillation | 27.6 | 45.3 | 72.9 | 214 |
| PROVE | Online | 88.0 | 88.0 | 1,126 |

Table 9: Complete pipeline compute costs. Generation and training costs
are GPU-hours. Online generation for PROVE is included in its 88.0
GPU-hours.

### A.5 Illustrative Examples of the PROVE Pipeline

To complement the method description in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Methods ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding"),
we provide end-to-end examples for the four supported Mutator
perturbation types: count, attribute, relation, and object. Each example
follows the perturb–verify–repair–verify trajectory:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(x,p)\xrightarrow{\text{Mutator }}p^{\prime}\xrightarrow{\text{Verifier}}(y_{1},r_{1})\xrightarrow{\text{Repairer }}\tilde{p}\xrightarrow{\text{Verifier}}(y_{2},r_{2}).
``` |  |

The Mutator emits a localized edit of the form
$`(\texttt{edit\_type},\texttt{target\_text},\texttt{replacement})`$,
which is applied to the clean caption $`p`$ to obtain the perturbed
caption $`p^{\prime}`$. The Verifier first judges whether $`p^{\prime}`$
matches the image and returns a binary decision $`y_{1}`$ with textual
feedback $`r_{1}`$. Conditioned on the image, the perturbed caption, and
this feedback, the Repairer directly generates a repaired caption
$`\tilde{p}`$. The Verifier is then invoked again to obtain
$`(y_{2},r_{2})`$. These examples illustrate how PROVE converts clean
image-caption pairs into grounded hard negatives and repair targets
without requiring a stronger external judge.

#### A.5.1 Count

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### A.5.2 Attribute

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### A.5.3 Relation

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### A.5.4 Object

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

##### Takeaways.

Across the four edit types, the same minimal-edit principle holds: the
Mutator flips exactly one semantic slot (count, attribute, relation, or
object) via a structured edit, the first Verifier pass localises the
mismatch via a short rationale, and the Repairer uses that rationale to
directly generate a faithful caption $`\tilde{p}`$ that, modulo at most
a few-token paraphrase (e.g. “standing indoors” $`\to`$ “indoors”),
matches the original $`p`$. The second Verifier pass closes the loop and
produces the success signal $`y_{2}`$ that drives the Repairer reward
$`r_{R}`$
(Eq. [12](#S3.E12 "In Repairer reward. ‣ 3.3 Verifier-Guided Rewards ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")).
Because perturbation is a discrete typed action while repair is
free-form caption generation, the two roles are not symmetric: the
Mutator is constrained to expose verifier blind spots along a known
axis, whereas the Repairer must recover the full caption from visual
evidence and verifier feedback, which is what makes repair an
operational form of verification.

Matched supervision settings. All comparisons use the same Qwen3.5-2B
initialization, 48k clean image-caption pairs, target-model optimization
budget, and evaluation protocol. Fixed typed negatives are generated
once and reused throughout training. External-judge distillation uses
judgments and textual feedback from a frozen larger VLM. Verifier
self-training uses self-generated labels without the Repairer or second
verification. This baseline isolates self-generated verifier supervision
under a matched image-text protocol; it is not a reproduction of
reasoning-oriented self-play methods with different tasks and
supervision.
Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
reports the matched supervision results. The same optimization budget
does not imply equal GPU-hours, since the methods execute different

### B.1 Component and Reward Ablations

Table [10](#A2.T10 "Table 10 ‣ B.1 Component and Reward Ablations ‣ Appendix B Controlled Supervision and Loop Ablations ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
isolates the role of static versus adaptive perturbations, the repair
loop, verifier feedback, the optimizer, and reward components. Removing
the Repairer and second verification produces the largest drop,
$`2.61/1.72`$ points on the compositional/broader averages. Removing
feedback costs $`1.68/1.19`$ points, indicating that repair benefits
from the verifier’s diagnosis. Both role rewards contribute: removing
the Mutator or Repairer reward costs $`1.82/1.27`$ or $`1.31/0.94`$
points, respectively. Removing the edit and repair costs reduces the

## Appendix C Independent Verification and Repeated-Run Analysis

### C.1 External Trajectory Audit

We audit a held-out trajectory set using labels produced outside the
self-play loop. These labels are never used for training, reward
computation, mutation generation, validation, or checkpoint selection.
The initial Qwen3.5-2B model and PROVE use the same role prompts and
deterministic editor.
Table [12](#A3.T12 "Table 12 ‣ C.1 External Trajectory Audit ‣ Appendix C Independent Verification and Repeated-Run Analysis ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
reports verifier accuracy on a fixed set and the quality of the
generated trajectories.

A valid localized perturbation introduces a real image-caption mismatch
confined to the intended edit. A correct verifier judgment identifies
whether the caption is faithful to the image. A faithful minimal repair
corrects the mismatch without introducing unsupported changes. A fully
valid trajectory requires all four stages to be correct: a real
localized mismatch, a correct diagnosis, a faithful minimal repair, and
a correct final judgment. The fully valid rate increases by $`23.4`$
points, while fixed-set verifier accuracy increases by $`7.8`$ points.
These external measurements support improved visual correctness, while
the shared-model setting still leaves possible self-verification bias
(Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")).

|                               |      |       |
|-------------------------------|------|-------|
| External audit                | Base | PROVE |
| Fixed-set verifier accuracy   | 75.8 | 83.6  |
| Valid localized perturbations | 82.4 | 92.1  |
| Correct verifier judgments    | 71.5 | 84.7  |
| Faithful minimal repairs      | 55.2 | 73.4  |
| Fully valid trajectories      | 40.8 | 64.2  |

Table 12: Complete external audit. All entries are percentages.
Fixed-set verifier accuracy and trajectory-quality rates are separate

## Appendix F Role Interfaces and Deterministic Editing

Role-conditioned interfaces. The Mutator receives the image and a
faithful caption and returns a single structured action with fields
edit_type, target_text, and replacement. The type is one of object,
attribute, count, or relation. The deterministic editor applies the
local replacement to construct the caption supplied to the first
Verifier. The Verifier receives the image and candidate caption and
produces a binary faithfulness decision with textual feedback; the
illustrative outputs in
Appendix [A.5](#A1.SS5 "A.5 Illustrative Examples of the PROVE Pipeline ‣ Appendix A Additional Experimental Details ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
use the fields answer and explanation. The Repairer receives the image,
perturbed caption, first decision, and explanation, and directly
generates a faithful caption with a minimal correction. The same
Verifier interface is used for the second verification. The complete
templates used in training are listed below.

Prompt templates. \<image\> marks the image input. Braced fields are
filled at run time: {p} is the clean caption $`p`$, {caption} is the
candidate caption ($`p^{\prime}`$ in the first verification and
$`\tilde{p}`$ in the second), {p’} is the perturbed caption, and {y1}
and {r1} are the first Verifier decision and explanation.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Output parsing. The Mutator output is parsed as
$`a_{M}=(\tau,t,\delta)`$ from edit_type, target_text, and replacement.
The Verifier output follows the format of
Appendix [A.5](#A1.SS5 "A.5 Illustrative Examples of the PROVE Pipeline ‣ Appendix A Additional Experimental Details ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding"):
a reasoning trace inside \<think\> tags followed by the JSON object.
answer$`=`$true gives $`y=1`$, answer$`=`$false gives $`y=0`$, and
explanation is the textual feedback $`r`$; the two verifications yield
$`(y_{1},r_{1})`$ and $`(y_{2},r_{2})`$. The Repairer output is the
repaired caption $`\tilde{p}`$ itself rather than an edit action.

Deterministic editing constraints. A valid action has a supported edit
type and nonempty target and replacement strings. The target must
identify one unambiguous span in the caption, and the replacement must
change it. Unsupported types, missing or ambiguous spans, unchanged
replacements, and edits that cannot be applied deterministically are
invalid. For a unique target span, the editor preserves the caption
prefix and suffix and replaces only that span.
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix F Role Interfaces and Deterministic Editing ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
specifies this local-edit interface. An invalid action receives the
invalid-action penalty $`-0.3`$ in
Table [5](#A1.T5 "Table 5 ‣ A.1 Training Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix A Additional Experimental Details ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
as its Mutator reward, and $`C_{M}`$ is not computed. Invalid edits do
not establish a valid negative example.

1: Caption $`p`$, structured action $`a_{M}=(\tau,t,\delta)`$

2: if $`a_{M}`$ cannot be parsed, $`\tau\notin\mathcal{T}`$, or
$`t,\delta`$ are missing or empty then

3:   return invalid action

4: end if

5: if $`t=\delta`$ or $`t`$ does not identify exactly one span in $`p`$
then

6:   return invalid action

7: end if

8: Write $`p=u\,t\,v`$ using the unique target occurrence

9: return $`p^{\prime}=u\,\delta\,v`$

Algorithm 1 Deterministic single-span editor specification

Reward weights.
Equations [10](#S3.E10 "In Mutator reward. ‣ 3.3 Verifier-Guided Rewards ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
and [12](#S3.E12 "In Repairer reward. ‣ 3.3 Verifier-Guided Rewards ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
instantiate
Equations [9](#S3.E9 "In Mutator reward. ‣ 3.3 Verifier-Guided Rewards ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
and [11](#S3.E11 "In Repairer reward. ‣ 3.3 Verifier-Guided Rewards ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
with $`R_{\mathrm{expose}}(y_{1})=\lambda_{1}\mathbb{1}[y_{1}=1]`$,
$`R_{\mathrm{hard}}(y_{2})=\lambda_{2}\mathbb{1}[y_{2}=0]`$, and
$`\lambda_{M}=\lambda_{3}`$ for the Mutator, and
$`R_{\mathrm{accept}}(y_{2})=\beta_{1}\mathbb{1}[y_{2}=1]`$,
$`R_{\mathrm{flip}}(y_{1},y_{2})=\beta_{2}\mathbb{1}[y_{1}\neq y_{2}]`$,
and $`\lambda_{R}=\beta_{3}`$ for the Repairer.
Table [19](#A6.T19 "Table 19 ‣ Appendix F Role Interfaces and Deterministic Editing ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
lists the weights used in all reported runs.

|                 |       |                                                     |
|-----------------|-------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| Weight          | Value | Term                                                |
| $`\lambda_{1}`$ | 1.0   | Perturbation not rejected by the first verification |
| $`\lambda_{2}`$ | 0.5   | Repaired caption still judged unfaithful            |
| $`\lambda_{3}`$ | 0.3   | Mutator edit cost $`C_{M}`$                         |
| $`\beta_{1}`$   | 0.8   | Repair accepted by the second verification          |
| $`\beta_{2}`$   | 0.7   | Judgment flip between the two verifications         |
| $`\beta_{3}`$   | 0.3   | Repairer rewriting cost $`C_{R}`$                   |

Table 19: Reward weights in
Equations [10](#S3.E10 "In Mutator reward. ‣ 3.3 Verifier-Guided Rewards ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
and [12](#S3.E12 "In Repairer reward. ‣ 3.3 Verifier-Guided Rewards ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding").

Cost terms. $`C_{M}`$ penalizes overly wide edit spans, normalized by
the character length of the clean caption:

|     |                                                             |     |      |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       C_{M}(a_{M})=2\cdot\frac{\mathrm{len}(t)}{\mathrm{len}(p)},
       ```                                                          |     | (16) |

with $`C_{M}=0`$ when $`t`$ or $`p`$ is empty. $`C_{R}`$ penalizes
unnecessary rewriting. Let $`T(\cdot)`$ split a caption on whitespace
and lowercase each token, and let $`\mathrm{lev}`$ be the token-level
Levenshtein distance:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
C_{R}(p^{\prime},\tilde{p})=\frac{\mathrm{lev}\big(T(p^{\prime}),T(\tilde{p})\big)}{\max\big(|T(p^{\prime})|,|T(\tilde{p})|\big)}.
``` |  | (17) |

$`C_{R}`$ is $`0`$ for identical captions, approaches $`1`$ for a
complete rewrite, and is set to $`1`$ when either caption has no tokens.

Reward and diagnostic interpretation.
Equations [10](#S3.E10 "In Mutator reward. ‣ 3.3 Verifier-Guided Rewards ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
and [12](#S3.E12 "In Repairer reward. ‣ 3.3 Verifier-Guided Rewards ‣ 3 Methods ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
specify the exposure, hardness, acceptance, judgment-flip, and cost
terms. The flip indicator $`\mathbb{1}[y_{1}\neq y_{2}]`$ rewards a
decision change; it is not independently a guarantee of a visually
correct repair. In particular, an evolving Verifier can accept an
incorrect caption, motivating the external audit in
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 External Trajectory Audit ‣ Appendix C Independent Verification and Repeated-Run Analysis ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding").
Repair success, structural alignment, and internal pass rate are
training diagnostics, whereas the external benchmark and audit labels
measure correctness independently. For a group of $`n=3`$ binary
outcomes, the empirical success fraction can take values
$`0,1/3,2/3,1`$. Its Bernoulli variance $`\bar{y}(1-\bar{y})`$ is
maximized at both $`1/3`$ and $`2/3`$;
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
plots the lower finite-group reference. This differs from the population
Bernoulli variance maximum at $`1/2`$ and is a diagnostic reference, not
an additional measurement or an external accuracy target.

## Appendix G Axis-level Gains, Qualitative Behavior, and Task Extensions

### G.1 Axis-level Gains

Axis-level gains.
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")(b)
summarizes where the gains of PROVE come from by aggregating benchmark
splits according to the visual-semantic capability they test. The
largest improvements appear on attribute and relation verification,
which are directly aligned with the typed perturbations used by the
Mutator. This pattern supports the intended training mechanism:
localized perturbations create visually checkable mismatches, forcing
the Verifier to diagnose fine-grained inconsistencies and the Repairer
to recover faithful captions. The positive gain on visual-detail
sensitivity further suggests that verifier-guided repair improves
localized evidence grounding beyond the core compositional benchmarks.
In contrast, object and color/order gains are smaller but still
positive, partly because the base model already performs strongly on
these axes.

### G.2 Qualitative Behavior and Failure Cases

Qualitative verifier behavior.
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.3 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Perturb, Repair, Verify: Self-Play Vision-Language Verifiers for Compositional Understanding")
provides representative examples of how the learned verifier changes
after self-play training. The base model often accepts captions or
answers that overlook a localized mismatch, such as an incorrect
relation, missing object evidence, wrong attribute, or counting error.
After PROVE training, the verifier produces judgments that better track
the relevant visual evidence and reject mismatches that the base model
misses. These examples indicate that PROVE does not merely improve
aggregate scores; it changes the verifier’s behavior in the intended
direction, making it more sensitive to the same visual-semantic factors
targeted by the perturb–verify–repair loop.

Failure cases. Our error analysis identifies four recurring settings:
small or occluded objects that are misperceived; ambiguous relations in
crowded scenes or unusual viewpoints; overlapping instances or unclear
counting conventions; and descriptions that require external knowledge
and invite language-prior judgments rather than image-grounded
verification. These settings can affect mutation validity, verifier
diagnosis, or repair quality. A localized edit may fail to create an
unambiguous mismatch, a Verifier may misidentify the relevant evidence,
or a Repairer may alter additional unsupported details. The independent
audit evaluates these stages separately rather than treating final
acceptance as sufficient evidence of a faithful trajectory.

Task extensions. The loop can be adapted when a task provides a
known-correct multimodal instance and a structured operation that
creates a verifiable error. For VQA, the Mutator could alter an answer,
rationale, or question condition and the Repairer could recover the
visually supported answer. For visual grounding, it could perturb a
region, bounding box, or referring phrase; for referring expressions, it
could alter target attributes or relations. The present experiments
establish caption-based verification and benchmark transfer, not
task-specific self-play training for these extensions.
````
